note.explanation: Relative atomic mass is a weighted average: isotopes that are more abundant have a greater effect on the average. Multiply each isotope’s mass by its percentage abundance, add the products, and divide by 100.
examples: For krypton, the textbook’s calculation gives a relative atomic mass of 83.7.
For lead, using the four isotope abundances in the in-text exercise gives 207.22.
note.simple: Imagine each isotope’s abundance as its share of the element. The most common isotope has the biggest influence on the average mass.
note.checkQuestion: An element has two isotopes of masses 80 and 85, with abundances 50% and 50%. What is its relative atomic mass?
note.title: Calculating relative atomic mass
steps: Write each isotope’s mass and abundance.
Multiply each mass by its percentage abundance.
note.answer: Relative atomic mass is calculated from the masses and abundances of an element’s isotopes.

options: The mass of an atom compared with the mass of a proton

rationales: This is incorrect because a proton is not the reference used for the relative atomic mass scale.

This is incorrect because the electron’s mass is not the reference for this scale.

mcqs.stem: What is the mass of one atomic mass unit (amu)?
rationales: This is incorrect because an amu is defined as one-twelfth, not one-half, of the mass of carbon-12.
This is incorrect because 12 amu is the mass of a carbon-12 atom on this scale.
This is correct because one amu is one-twelfth the mass of a carbon-12 atom.
This is incorrect because 24 amu is not the definition of an amu.

options: The isotope with the greatest mass
The isotope with the lowest mass
All isotopes contribute equally, whatever their abundance
The relative isotopic masses and their abundances
mcqs.stem: Which information is needed to calculate an element’s relative atomic mass from its isotopes?
rationales: This is incorrect because the heaviest isotope alone does not determine the average.
This is incorrect because the lightest isotope alone does not determine the average.
This is incorrect because isotope contributions depend on their abundances.
This is correct because the calculation uses each isotope’s mass and its abundance.

mcqs.stem: An element has isotopes of masses 24 and 25 with abundances 50% each. What is its relative atomic mass?
rationales: This is incorrect because it is below the average of the two equally abundant isotope masses.
This is correct because (24 × 50 + 25 × 50) / 100 = 24.5.
This is incorrect because the average of 24 and 25 is 24.5, not 25.0.
This is incorrect because the weighted products must be divided by 100.

mcqs.stem: An element has isotopes of masses 82 and 84, with abundances 50% and 50%. What is its relative atomic mass?
rationales: This is incorrect because it is below the average of the two isotope masses.
This is incorrect because 82 is the mass of only the lighter isotope.
This is correct because the two equally abundant isotopes give an average of (82 + 84) / 2 = 83.
This is incorrect because 84 is the mass of only the heavier isotope.

options: The average is pulled more towards the mass of the more abundant isotope.
The average is always exactly halfway between the isotope masses.
The average is always the mass of the heaviest isotope.
The average does not depend on isotope abundance.
mcqs.stem: How does a more abundant isotope affect an element’s relative atomic mass?
rationales: This is correct because the more abundant isotope contributes more to the weighted average.
This is incorrect because the average is halfway between the masses only when the abundances are equal.
This is incorrect because the average is not necessarily equal to the heaviest isotope’s mass.
This is incorrect because isotope abundance is essential to the calculation.

explain.title: Why relative atomic mass is useful
explain.body: Atoms are extremely small, so their masses are compared on a scale rather than measured in kilograms for ordinary chemical calculations. The scale lets chemists compare atom masses and work out the ratios for chemical reactions.

explain.title: The atomic mass unit
explain.body: The textbook defines the atomic mass unit as one-twelfth the mass of an atom of carbon-12. On this scale, a carbon-12 atom has a mass of exactly 12.

explain.title: Finding the average from isotopes
explain.body: An element’s isotopes can have different masses and different natural abundances. Multiply each relative isotopic mass by its percentage abundance, add the products, and divide by 100 to find the relative atomic mass.

explain.title: When an isotope mass is unknown
explain.body: Use the same weighted-average formula, but write the unknown isotope mass as a variable. Substitute the known average and abundances, then rearrange the equation to find the unknown.

mistakes: Adding isotope masses without weighting them by their abundances.
Pairing an isotope mass with the wrong abundance.
Forgetting to divide the weighted sum by 100.
Using an abundance as a whole number in the formula but forgetting that it is a percentage.
For an unknown isotope mass, stopping at the equation instead of showing how the variable is isolated.
